a: the word of the LORD came
t: The LORD, and a prophet's word
p: The divine name YHWH is written "the LORD"; "the word of the LORD came" opens each dated message.
b: The Hebrew has the four letters YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God, which most English Bibles print as "the LORD" in capitals. "God" (Elohim) is the common word. In Haggai the word comes "through" the prophet (literally "by the hand of"); here it comes "to" Zechariah (el), the wording Jeremiah and Ezekiel use for their calls. The formula opens 1:1, 1:7 and 7:1, and the shorter forms at 4:8, 6:9, 7:4, 7:8, 8:1 and 8:18 mark the separate messages. All the dates in the book are in the reign of Darius I, the same Persian king as Haggai's.

a: In the eighth month of the second year of Darius
p: The first date is late October to late November 520 BC, between Haggai's second and third messages.
b: Darius I took the Persian throne in 522 BC after months of revolt and spent his first years winning it back. By the usual conversion to our calendar, Haggai's messages ran from 29 August to 18 December 520 BC (Haggai 1:1; Haggai 2:10, 20). Zechariah's first word falls in the eighth month, late October to late November 520, between them. The work on the Temple had restarted on 21 September (Haggai 1:14-15). Zechariah begins not with building but with the people's relation to the LORD.
r: Ezra 4:24; Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14-15; Haggai 1:1; Haggai 1:14-15; Haggai 2:1

a: Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo
p: Ezra calls him only "son of Iddo"; the book adds Berechiah. The name means "the LORD remembers."
b: Zechariah (Zekaryah, "the LORD remembers") was a common name; about thirty men carry it in the Bible. Ezra names this prophet "Zechariah son of Iddo" (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14), and Nehemiah 12:16 lists a Zechariah as head of the priestly house of Iddo, so he was probably a priest as well as a prophet. The book gives his father as Berechiah, perhaps because the grandson succeeded to the house when Berechiah died young. Matthew 23:35 names "Zechariah son of Berechiah" as a murdered man killed between the sanctuary and the altar, but 2 Chronicles 24:20-22 has Zechariah son of Jehoiada. Which man Matthew means, and whether he has joined the two, is debated; see the topic on the two Zechariahs.
r: Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14; Nehemiah 12:4; Nehemiah 12:16; 2 Chronicles 24:20-22; Matthew 23:35; Isaiah 8:2

a: The LORD was angry with your ancestors, truly angry
p: Literally "the LORD was angry with an anger"; the book's first sentence is about a judgment already finished.
b: The Hebrew puts the verb and its noun side by side (qatsaf ... qetsef, "was angry with anger"). It is the book's first statement, and it is in the past tense: the exile is God's judgment on the earlier generations, and it has happened. The same noun returns at 1:15 ("I am very angry with the nations"), 7:12 ("a great wrath came") and 8:14 ("when your ancestors made me angry"). The book's whole movement is from that anger to the promise in 1:16 and 8:2-3 that the LORD has come back with compassion and jealousy for Zion.
orig: קָצַף ... קֶצֶף (qatsaf ... qetsef), 'was angry with anger'

a: The LORD of Armies says this
p: The title the book uses most often for God, dozens of times in 14 chapters.
b: The Hebrew is YHWH tseva'ot. Tseva'ot means "armies" or "hosts." Scholars differ on whose armies are meant: Israel's armies, the angels, the stars, or all the powers of heaven and earth. The Plain keeps "the LORD of Armies" everywhere, as the Bible Scroll does in Haggai and the other prophets; the Greek of the New Testament writes kyrios sabaoth (Romans 9:29; James 5:4), and the Greek of Zechariah here has Kyrios Pantokrator or "Lord of the powers." The title fits the book's setting, a tiny province of the world's largest empire, where the claim is that the real commander of armies is the God who sends horsemen through the earth (1:10) and chariots from between mountains (6:1-8). "Says this" translates koh amar, the prophet's messenger formula.

t: "Return to me, and I will return to you"
p: The call to turn back (shuv) is the book's opening message and is answered by the LORD's own return.
b: Shuv means "turn" or "return," and it carries the whole book. Here people are told to return to the LORD; at 1:16 and 8:3 the LORD says that he has returned to Jerusalem and Zion; at 8:15 "I have turned again" to do good; at 1:6 the ancestors "turned back" after judgment. The call matches earlier prophets (Jeremiah 3:12-14; Hosea 14:1-2) and is picked up by Malachi 3:7, where the promise is nearly the same. In the text the call to return (1:3-6) comes first and the LORD's comfort (1:13-17) after it, but the two belong to one turning: the LORD promises to return to those who return, and 1:16 says that he has returned. The book does not say which turning comes first, and it does not make repentance a way to earn the return.
r: Jeremiah 3:12; Hosea 14:1; Joel 2:12-13; Malachi 3:7; Zechariah 1:16; Zechariah 8:3; Zechariah 8:15

p: Ne'um is a noun, "an utterance of the LORD."
b: The Plain's "the LORD declares" translates ne'um YHWH, literally "the utterance of the LORD." It is a noun, set off at the end of a clause as a signature on the speech. The book uses it in 1:3, 1:4, 1:16, 2:5, 2:6, 2:10, 3:9, 3:10, 5:4, 8:6, 8:11, 8:14 and 8:17. It is found throughout the prophets, and Jeremiah uses it most.
orig: נְאֻם יְהוָה (ne'um YHWH), 'the utterance of YHWH'

p: A phrase used here and at 7:7 and 7:12 for the prophets before the exile, who called for the same turning.
b: The Hebrew hanevi'im harishonim means "the first (or former) prophets," those before the exile. Zechariah treats them as a body whose message was consistent: turn from evil ways and deeds. The words he gives them are close to the wording of Jeremiah's call (Jeremiah 18:11; 25:5; 35:15), and 2 Kings 17:13 says the LORD warned Israel and Judah "by every prophet." He uses the phrase three times, always for the generation whose words, he says, outlived them (1:6) and whose message 7:7-12 repeats. The phrase later became a name for the Former Prophets (Joshua to Kings) in Jewish usage, but here it is a historical description, not a book title.
r: Jeremiah 18:11; Jeremiah 25:4-5; Jeremiah 35:15; 2 Kings 17:13; Zechariah 7:7; Zechariah 7:12

a: the prophets, do they live forever?
t: Who is dead, and what lives?
p: The verse asks about both the ancestors and the prophets; readers differ on whom "the prophets" are.
b: The Hebrew is a pair of questions with no answer given. Everyone knows the ancestors are dead. "Do the prophets live forever?" can mean the earlier prophets, who died too, or Haggai and Zechariah now, who will also die; in both cases the point of 1:6 follows, that the prophets are mortal and their words are not. A few readers hear the question as spoken by doubters: your ancestors are gone and so are the old prophets, so why listen? The next verse answers all of these readings: the words outlast the speakers and "overtook" the ancestors. The verse is also a reminder that the book is addressed to people who had lived through exactly what the earlier prophets said would happen.

a: did they not overtake your ancestors
p: The verb is the one Deuteronomy uses for blessings and curses that run someone down.
b: Hissigu ("overtook") is covenant language. In Deuteronomy 28 the blessings come on Israel and "overtake" it if it obeys (28:2), and the curses pursue it and "overtake" it if it does not (28:15, 45). Zechariah says the earlier prophets' words did exactly that: they were not empty. The exiles' own confession in this verse, "he has done with us as our ways and our deeds deserved," is the verdict of Lamentations 1:18 and Nehemiah 9:33. The point is not blame alone: only a people who admit the word was true can hear that the same LORD has now turned to them with comfort (1:13).

t: The month names and the date
p: Shebat (January-February) is a Babylonian month name; this date is 15 February 519 BC by the usual conversion.
b: The Hebrew Bible first numbered its months ("the eleventh month"); the names Shebat, Kislev, Adar and others came from Babylon during the exile and are used only in Persian-period writings (Zechariah 1:7; 7:1; Nehemiah 1:1; Esther 3:7). The twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month converts to 15 February 519 BC by the usual conversion, five months after the work on the Temple began (Haggai 1:14-15) and about two months after Haggai's last message (Haggai 2:20). The visions from 1:8 to 6:8 are dated to this one night, and the prophet is woken between visions (4:1).

p: The visions run from 1:8 to 6:8, one night, in a fixed pattern of seeing, asking and an angel's answer.
b: The eight visions are the horsemen among the myrtles (1:8-17), the four horns and four craftsmen (1:18-21), the man with the measuring cord (2:1-5), Joshua and the Accuser (3:1-10), the lampstand and the olive trees (4:1-14), the flying scroll (5:1-4), the woman in the ephah (5:5-11) and the four chariots (6:1-8). Some count seven by joining the two scenes of chapter 5; others find the oracles of 2:6-13 and 6:9-15 outside the visions. Each vision follows the same steps: the prophet sees, asks "What is this?", and is answered by the angel. They are arranged in a ring: horses at the start, chariots at the end; the earth quiet (1:11), the LORD's spirit at rest in the north (6:8). The topic on the night visions lays out the structure.
r: Zechariah 1:7; Zechariah 4:1; Zechariah 6:8; Ezekiel 40:1-4; Daniel 7:1; Amos 7:1-9

a: a man riding a red horse
t: The rider and the angel of the LORD
p: The rider is the same figure as "the angel of the LORD" in 1:11, which makes him a heavenly being.
b: In 1:10 "the man standing among the myrtle trees" speaks, and in 1:11 the riders report to "the angel of the LORD who was standing among the myrtle trees," so the man and the angel are one. Most commentators see an angelic captain of the patrol. The idea of the angel of the LORD as a pre-incarnate Christ runs through Christian reading. Calvin, on 1:7-11, says that if this angel is taken to be Christ, the idea fits the usual language of Scripture, since Christ is the head of the angels, and he allows that one angel may have had a pre-eminence so that the prophet would think of the Redeemer (Calvin, lectures on Zechariah 1:7-11). Jewish readers have usually taken the figure as an angel. The colors have no stated meaning: red, reddish-brown and white are the colors of the four horses in 6:1-3, and Revelation 6:1-8 draws a sequence from a similar set, but it does not use the same colors in the same order.
r: Zechariah 1:10-11; Zechariah 6:1-3; Genesis 16:7; Exodus 3:2; Judges 6:11-12; Revelation 6:1-8

p: The myrtle (hadas) is an evergreen that grows in valleys; the Plain does not say why the scene sits among them.
b: The myrtle grows in damp hollows in Palestine and was used for the booths of the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8:15), and God promised to plant it in the wilderness (Isaiah 41:19; Isaiah 55:13). Esther's Hebrew name Hadassah comes from the same word (Esther 2:7). The myrtle is a symbol of lasting life and, in this vision, of a hidden grove where the heavenly riders gather, outside the sight of the world. Scholars suggest that the grove is a hint of the garden of the divine presence, that the myrtle recalls the Temple's missing trees, or that it is simply part of a landscape. The text does not decide. The Greek has "mountains" here (see the variant).

a: The angel who spoke with me
p: A guide who explains the visions; the Hebrew says "the angel who speaks in me."
b: The interpreting angel is a figure of later prophecy. Ezekiel is led through the new temple by a man with a measuring rod (Ezekiel 40:3-4), Daniel is explained by Gabriel (Daniel 8:16; 9:21-22) and by another heavenly figure (Daniel 10), and the writings called 1 Enoch (outside the 66 books) give the seer a named angel such as Uriel. In Zechariah the angel is "the angel who spoke with me" in every vision, the Plain's fixed English. The Hebrew preposition bet is literally "in": "the angel who speaks in me." The Greek has the same "in me." It may point to inspiration inside the prophet, but it is also the ordinary word "with." Revelation takes up the same guide figure (Revelation 17:1; Revelation 21:9; Revelation 22:8).
r: Ezekiel 40:3; Daniel 8:16; Daniel 9:21; Revelation 17:1; Revelation 21:9; Zechariah 1:19; Zechariah 2:3; Zechariah 4:1

p: The riders do what the Accuser does in Job: they walk the earth and report.
b: The Hebrew verb is hithallekh, "to walk back and forth." In Job 1:7 and Job 2:2 the Accuser answers God that he comes "from ranging across the earth, and walking all around it." Zechariah's riders do the same task and report in 1:11. The picture is that of an inspection tour that reports back, turned here to the heavenly court. The "eyes of the LORD" that "run to and fro through the whole earth" (2 Chronicles 16:9; Zechariah 4:10) are the same idea. The Accuser of 3:1 appears two visions later, as if one of this council.
r: Job 1:7; Job 2:2; 2 Chronicles 16:9; Zechariah 3:1; Zechariah 4:10; Zechariah 6:7

t: The quiet that was bad news
p: In February 519 the Persian world was calm, which was a problem for those hoping the LORD would shake the nations.
b: Darius had taken the throne in 522 and spent his early years putting down revolts. Haggai had promised that the LORD would soon "shake the heavens and the earth" (Haggai 2:6, 21-22). Instead the earth is "settled and quiet" (yoshevet veshoqetet). The angel's reaction is the next verse: how long? The report sets up the book's central tension: the world is quiet, the Temple is half-built, and the promise of a greater glory (Haggai 2:9) is not yet visible. Some read the revolts of 522-521 as the shaking that Haggai meant; the quiet then shows it was over.

a: how long will you refuse to have compassion on Jerusalem
p: A heavenly being asks the lament question of the Psalms, and the LORD answers with comfort.
b: "How long?" ('ad matay) is the cry of lament in the Psalms (Psalm 74:10; Psalm 79:5; Psalm 80:4; Psalm 89:46) and in Habakkuk 1:2. Here the angel of the LORD asks it for Jerusalem, and the LORD answers him, not the prophet (1:13). The angel is an intercessor, a being who speaks to God on behalf of people on earth, as in Job 33:23-26, Tobit 12:12-15 (a book that is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians and not for Protestants) and Revelation 8:3-4. In the book's own terms, the point is that heaven has already sided with Jerusalem.

p: Jeremiah's seventy years can be counted from 605, from 586, or as a round number; Zechariah counts to about 519.
b: Jeremiah said Babylon would rule the nations for seventy years and that the exiles would then return (Jeremiah 25:11-12; Jeremiah 29:10). The Chronicler counts the seventy years from the Temple's burning to Cyrus (2 Chronicles 36:20-21), and Daniel read the number in the scrolls (Daniel 9:2). Zechariah says the LORD has been indignant with Jerusalem and the cities of Judah for seventy years, and he repeats the number at 7:5. From 586 (the Temple burned) to 519 is 67 years; from Jeremiah's 605 to Cyrus's decree in 538 is 67 as well. The number may be exact, rounded, or the symbolic span of a lifetime (Psalm 90:10). Zechariah's use is the plainest: it is the time that has now passed since the Temple fell.

p: The word is nichumim, from nacham, which is also the verb for the LORD changing his mind.
b: The noun nichumim ("comfort") comes from the root nacham. In one form (the piel) the root means to comfort, as in Isaiah 40:1; in another (the niphal) it means to change one's mind or feel regret, as in 8:14, where the LORD says that he "did not change his mind" about sending the harm. The two senses are connected: to comfort is to turn toward someone. Zechariah uses the root for comfort in 1:13 and 1:17, and for the LORD's change of mind in 8:14, set against his turning again in 8:15. In the book as written the call to return (1:3-6) comes before the comfort (1:13-17); the two belong to the same turning, as in Isaiah 40, where comfort and the call to prepare stand side by side.

a: I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion, with a great jealousy
p: God's "jealousy" (qin'ah) is the fierce loyalty of a husband for a wife, not envy.
b: Qin'ah covers a range from zeal to jealousy. When it is God's, it is fierce commitment to a covenant partner and anger at rivals: "I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God" (Exodus 20:5). In the prophets the husband image gives it its meaning (Ezekiel 16:38, 42; Hosea 2). Here the jealousy works for Jerusalem against the nations (1:15). It returns at 8:2, where it is joined with chemah, "fury." The Greek has ezelōka "I have been zealous," and Paul uses the same Greek word, zēlos "zeal," of his own concern for the church (2 Corinthians 11:2).
r: Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:14; Joel 2:18; Nahum 1:2; Ezekiel 39:25; Zechariah 8:2; 2 Corinthians 11:2

a: I was only a little angry, but they helped make the harm worse
t: The tool that went too far
p: The nations were the LORD's instrument, but they went beyond what he asked.
b: The idea is old in the prophets: God uses a nation to punish his people, then judges it for how it did the job. Assyria is the rod of his anger and then is cut down for its pride (Isaiah 10:5-15). Babylon was given his people but showed them no mercy (Isaiah 47:6). Judgment on the nations that were "at ease" (hasha'ananim) is the other side of comfort for Jerusalem; it matches the promise in 2:8-9 that the nations that plundered Israel will themselves be plundered. Obadiah and Nahum make the same turn on Edom and Assyria.

a: a measuring line will be stretched across Jerusalem
p: A line that once measured a city for destruction now measures it for building.
b: The Hebrew qav is a builder's measuring line. Elsewhere the LORD stretches a line over a city to mark it for destruction (2 Kings 21:13; Isaiah 34:11; Lamentations 2:8). Here the same act becomes a promise to rebuild (compare Jeremiah 31:38-40; Ezekiel 40:3). It leads straight to the next vision, where a man goes to measure Jerusalem (2:1-2). The written text has a spelling difference: the consonantal text (Ketiv) reads veqavah and the margin (Qere) reads veqav; both mean "a measuring line," and the Plain does not need an entry. The topic on the measuring line follows the image through the Bible.
r: 2 Kings 21:13; Isaiah 34:11; Lamentations 2:8; Jeremiah 31:38-40; Ezekiel 40:3; Zechariah 2:1-2; Revelation 11:1

a: once more he will choose Jerusalem
p: The language of election, used for David and for the city, is repeated at 2:12 and 3:2.
b: The Hebrew verb bachar ("choose") is the word Deuteronomy uses for "the place the LORD will choose" for his name (Deuteronomy 12:5), and the books of Kings and the Psalms say he chose Jerusalem and David (1 Kings 11:13, 32; Psalm 132:13). The exile looked like the end of that choice. Zechariah says it is not: the LORD will "again" choose Jerusalem. The same promise returns at 2:12 and 3:2 ("the LORD, who has chosen Jerusalem"), and the Hebrew word for "again" ('od) occurs four times in 1:17, the book's way of saying that what was lost is returning.

t: Verse numbers and the vision formula
p: In the Hebrew Bible, English 1:18-21 are 2:1-4, so the Hebrew chapter 2 begins at English 1:18 and runs to English 2:13 (Hebrew 2:1-17).
b: The English verses 1:18-21 are Hebrew 2:1-4, and English 2:1-13 is Hebrew 2:5-17. So the Hebrew chapter 1 has 17 verses (English 1:1-17) and the Hebrew chapter 2 has 17 (English 1:18 to 2:13), as the Hebrew-to-English verse map in the source text shows. Everything else in the book numbers the same in English and Hebrew; the Greek (Swete's text) follows the Hebrew numbering. This site uses the English numbers, so "2:10" here is "2:14" in a Jewish Bible (the haftarah for the Sabbath of Hanukkah, Zechariah 2:14 to 4:7 in Hebrew numbers, begins at the English 2:10). "I looked up and saw" translates va'essa 'einai va'ere, "and I lifted up my eyes and saw," the formula used in 1:18; 2:1; 5:1, 5, 9; 6:1. The Plain keeps one English for it.

p: A horn is a symbol of power. The four are the powers that scattered Judah; the text does not name them.
b: Horns stand for strength throughout the Bible (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 75:10; Daniel 7:7-8; Daniel 8:3-8). The angel names what they did: they "scattered Judah, Israel and Jerusalem" (1:19), so they are the nations that invaded Israel and Judah. "Four" can be a number of totality, the four directions, the four winds that appear in 2:6 and 6:5. Many Jewish and Christian interpreters match them to the four empires of Daniel 2 and 7 (Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece and a fourth: Rome in the usual Christian reading, and in many Jewish readings, Rome or Edom). Modern historians propose Assyria, Egypt, Babylon and another, or simply all the enemies of Israel. The vision's point is clear without a list.

p: The Hebrew charashim are smiths or carpenters; the Talmud makes them four figures of the end.
b: Charashim are skilled workers in metal, wood or stone (Isaiah 44:12; Isaiah 54:16 "the smith who blows on the coals"). The Greek has tektonas, "builders," and the Latin Vulgate fabros, "smiths." The craftsmen come "to terrify the horns" and knock them down. A talmudic teaching (Sukkah 52b) says the four craftsmen are the Messiah son of David, the Messiah son of Joseph, Elijah, and the righteous priest. This reads the verse as a prophecy of the end; it is a Jewish interpretive tradition, not what the vision first said. Christian readers have found the four in the apostles, the four evangelists, or the rulers of the church. The vision itself says only that every horn has an answer.

a: a man holding a measuring cord
p: A man with a measuring cord also leads Ezekiel through the new temple and John through the new Jerusalem.
b: The man is an angel in human form. Ezekiel is shown a man with a flax cord and a measuring rod (Ezekiel 40:3), and in Revelation a measuring rod is given to John (Revelation 11:1) and an angel measures the new Jerusalem with a gold rod (Revelation 21:15). Zechariah's man goes to measure Jerusalem. The angels then say the city needs no measurement because no wall can contain it (2:4). The scene sits in a city whose walls, in 519, were still broken down (Nehemiah 1:3; Nehemiah 2:17).

p: The angel tells another angel to run to "this young man"; the Hebrew does not say who he is.
b: The na'ar ("young man") may be the man with the measuring cord, who is told to stop; or the prophet himself, who would be a young man in 519 (compare Jeremiah 1:6, where Jeremiah calls himself a na'ar); or an angel. The Greek has neanian ekeinon, "that young man." If it is the measurer, the message tells him his work is wrong: do not measure a city that will have no walls. If it is Zechariah, the angel's message is for the people. The sense of the message is the same either way. Modern commentators are about evenly divided.

p: The promise is a city so full that no wall could hold it; in 519 the real city's walls were still down.
b: Perazot are open, unwalled villages (Ezekiel 38:11; Esther 9:19). Jerusalem will be inhabited like such villages, with people and animals spilling past any line. The Greek reads it as "fruitfully" (katakarpōs, "it will be inhabited with abundance"). Nehemiah, in 445 BC, gets permission to rebuild the wall (Nehemiah 2:17; Nehemiah 6:15), so the city was not left without one. Jewish and Christian readers have taken the promise as a hope that the LORD, not stone, is the city's protection (the next verse), and as a promise of the end of days.

a: a wall of fire around her
p: The LORD is the wall and the glory: fire like the wilderness pillar, and the glory that left the Temple in Ezekiel.
b: The pair "wall of fire" and "glory" recalls the pillar of fire and cloud that led Israel (Exodus 13:21-22; Exodus 40:34-38) and the fire around Elisha in 2 Kings 6:17. Isaiah 4:5 promised a cloud by day and the glow of fire by night over Mount Zion. In Ezekiel the glory of the LORD left the first Temple (Ezekiel 10:18-19; Ezekiel 11:22-23) and returns to the new one (Ezekiel 43:1-5). Zechariah's "inside her I will be her glory" is that return. Haggai promised that the LORD would fill the new house with glory (Haggai 2:7, 9). So the safe place is the presence of the LORD himself, not a rebuilt wall.
r: Exodus 13:21; 2 Kings 6:17; Isaiah 4:5; Ezekiel 10:18; Ezekiel 43:1-5; Haggai 2:7-9

p: Hoy is usually "woe"; here it is a summons to get up and leave.
b: Hoy began as the cry at a funeral ("Alas!"), became the prophets' "Woe to ..." and can also be a plain call for attention, as in Isaiah 55:1. In 2:6-7 it is a summons, so the Plain says "Come!" The summons is to the Jews who were still in Babylon ('the land of the north', where enemy armies entered Israel: Jeremiah 1:14; Jeremiah 3:18; Jeremiah 6:22). Many had stayed after Cyrus's decree. The call echoes Isaiah's "go out from Babylon" (Isaiah 48:20; Isaiah 52:11) and Jeremiah's "flee from the midst of Babylon" (Jeremiah 51:6, 45). Revelation 18:4 uses the same image against a later Babylon: "Come out of her, my people."

p: A city or people is spoken of as a daughter: Daughter Zion, Daughter Babylon.
b: Bat ("daughter") before the name of a city or people is a poetic way of speaking of it as a woman. The Plain keeps it as "Daughter Zion," "Daughter Babylon," as in Isaiah and Lamentations (Isaiah 47:1; Lamentations 1:6; Psalm 137:8). Here the phrase "you who live with Daughter Babylon" is addressed to Zion herself: Zion is the people of Jerusalem, and they are living with Babylon. The call asks them to leave.

t: Who is sent, and what is "after glory"?
p: The speaker says "the LORD sent me," yet speaks as the LORD; the phrase "after glory" is also unclear.
b: Three hard points. Who speaks? The speaker says the LORD of Armies "sent me" (2:8, 9, 11) and also says "I will make my home among you" (2:10). Views: the prophet speaking for God; the angel of the LORD; or a figure who is God's own agent. Christian writers since the Fathers have heard the Son sent by the Father; Jewish commentators generally take the prophet or an angel. What does "after glory" mean? It may mean "after the glory has appeared," "in pursuit of glory" or "for the sake of glory." The Greek has opisō doxēs, "after glory," and the Vulgate post gloriam. The Plain keeps the Hebrew words. Where does the verse end? Some join "after glory" to the previous line; the Plain puts it with "he sent me."

p: A rare word for the pupil, with an unclear "his": the LORD's own eye, or the touching nation's.
b: Bavat 'eno is found only here; the usual word for the pupil is 'ishon, as in Deuteronomy 32:10 and Psalm 17:8 ("the pupil of the eye"). Whose eye? The Hebrew text, 4Q80 (a Dead Sea scroll of the Twelve) and the Greek all say "his eye." The Vulgate has "my eye" (oculi mei), which makes the LORD the one touched. If "his" is the LORD's, the verse says to touch Israel is to touch the most guarded part of God. If "his" is the toucher's, it says that harming Israel is harming oneself. The commonest view takes it as God's eye with the speaker changing person in mid-verse, as Hebrew prophecy often does.

t: Making a home: the root of Shekhinah
p: The verb shakan is the root of the Jewish term Shekhinah, God's dwelling presence.
b: The verb is shakan, "to dwell, to settle," the word for God's presence in the Tabernacle (Exodus 25:8; Exodus 29:45-46). The later Jewish word Shekhinah for the divine presence comes from it. The Plain says "make my home." Zechariah's promise (2:10, 2:11; 8:3) is the return of the presence that had left (Ezekiel 10-11; Ezekiel 43:7). John 1:14 says the Word "lived among us" using the Greek eskēnōsen, which sounds like shakan and means "pitched his tent." The Christian reading finds the promise fulfilled in Jesus; the Jewish reading finds it in the Temple and in the world to come.
r: Exodus 25:8; Exodus 29:45; Ezekiel 43:7; Zephaniah 3:14-17; John 1:14; Revelation 21:3

a: On that day many nations will attach themselves to the LORD
p: Nations become "my people," in the words once said of Israel. How that fits with Judah as the LORD's "portion" (2:12) is debated.
b: The verb nilvu ("join") is used of foreigners who attach themselves to the LORD in Isaiah 56:3, 6 and of nations joining in Jeremiah 50:5. The words "they will become my people" are the covenant formula first said to Israel (Exodus 6:7), and Hosea turns it to the unloved (Hosea 2:23). Zechariah applies them to many nations. The next verse says that the LORD takes Judah as his own portion. Jewish readings keep the two distinct: the nations come to the God of Israel (8:20-23). Christian readings often see the church of Jews and Gentiles (Ephesians 2:11-22). Dispensationalist readings, as a general pattern not tied here to one named teacher, keep Israel and the nations apart. The card on 8:23 sets the Catholic and Reformed views side by side.
r: Isaiah 56:3; Isaiah 56:6; Jeremiah 50:5; Hosea 2:23; Exodus 6:7; Zechariah 8:20-23; Ephesians 2:11-22

p: The only place the Hebrew Bible calls Judah's soil "the holy land."
b: Admat haqodesh ("the soil of holiness") is a unique phrase. Moses stood on admat qodesh, "holy ground" (Exodus 3:5), but the title "the holy land" for the whole country appears here and in Wisdom of Solomon 12:3 (a Greek book that Catholics and Orthodox count as Scripture and Protestants do not). The Jews of later centuries gave the phrase a large place; "Holy Land" is still a common name for the region. In Zechariah it does not make the whole land holy for all times: it says the LORD takes Judah as his portion on the ground where his presence will return.
r: Exodus 3:5; Psalm 78:54; Zechariah 8:3; Wisdom of Solomon 12:3

p: The LORD is said to have been roused, as if he had been asleep or sitting still.
b: The Hebrew ne'or means "has been stirred up." The language of an inactive God being roused is bold: the Psalms ask him to wake (Psalm 44:23; Psalm 78:65) and Isaiah calls on his arm to "wake" (Isaiah 51:9). Here the LORD has acted. The command "hush" (has, found also in Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7) calls for the silence due to a king or judge on entering. The verse is a bridge to the next vision, where the court is in session. Some Christian readers hear in it the stir before the Lord's appearing; Revelation 8:1 has half an hour of silence in heaven.
r: Psalm 44:23; Psalm 78:65; Isaiah 51:9; Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7; Revelation 8:1

t: Joshua, the high priest of the return
p: Joshua son of Jehozadak, called Jeshua in Ezra, led the priests who came back; his grandfather was killed by Babylon.
b: Joshua (Yehoshua, shortened to Yeshua or Jeshua in Ezra and Nehemiah) is named with Zerubbabel in Haggai (1:1, 12, 14; 2:2, 4) and in Ezra 3:2 and 5:2. His father Jehozadak went into exile in 586 (1 Chronicles 6:15), and his grandfather, the chief priest Seraiah, had been executed at Riblah (2 Kings 25:18-21). He is "the high priest," literally "the great priest" (hakohen hagadol), the title the law already uses (Leviticus 21:10) and that Haggai and Zechariah give him. The name Joshua is the same as the Greek Iēsous, Jesus, and the Greek of this verse writes Iēsous. Justin Martyr read the scene as a picture of Jesus Christ and his people (Dialogue with Trypho 115-116); that is reception, not the Hebrew's meaning.
r: Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:2; Ezra 5:2; 1 Chronicles 6:15; 2 Kings 25:18-21; Haggai 2:2

p: Hassatan has the article, so it is a title ("the adversary"), as in Job 1-2. Without it (1 Chronicles 21:1) it is "Satan."
b: Satan is a common noun meaning "adversary" or "opponent," from a verb that means to oppose or accuse (it is the verb in the last words of this verse, "to accuse him"). With the article it means "the adversary" in a courtroom: the one who brings the charge. This is the Plain's rendering in Job 1-2 as well. In 1 Chronicles 21:1, where there is no article, it is a name, "Satan." The Greek of Zechariah has ho diabolos, "the slanderer," the word the New Testament uses for the devil. In Psalm 109:6 an accuser (satan) stands at the right hand of the person on trial, the place where the prosecutor stood; Zechariah 3:1 uses the same picture. In Numbers 22:22, 32 the angel who blocks Balaam is "a satan." Whether this accuser is already the devil of the New Testament is the question of the next note.
r: Job 1:6; Job 2:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1; Psalm 109:6; Numbers 22:22; Revelation 12:10

a: May the LORD rebuke you, Accuser!
t: Who is the Accuser, and who rebukes him?
p: A courtroom scene: the Accuser charges, and the LORD answers. Whether this is the devil is read in different ways.
b: The scene. A heavenly court has the high priest as defendant, the Accuser as prosecutor and the angel of the LORD as judge. The LORD himself answers the Accuser, in the third person, "may the LORD rebuke you," as the angel does in Jude 9 ("The Lord rebuke you"). The Accuser. Jewish readers take him as a prosecuting angel, a member of the council who tests; in Job the same figure acts only with God's leave. Critical scholars see an officer of the heavenly court who develops, in the centuries after the exile, into a figure of evil. Christian readers from the Fathers on take him as the devil, the accuser of Revelation 12:10. Paul answers the same question with Romans 8:33-34: "Who will accuse the people God has chosen?" The Catholic Catechism (391-395) sees in the tempter a fallen angel called Satan or the devil, a creature made good who became evil by his own doing, and Calvin on 3:1-2 identifies the opponent with the devil. The real contrast is between that reading and the Jewish and critical ones above, so this passage has no traditions card.

a: a piece of firewood snatched from the fire
t: A stick snatched from the fire
p: A piece of wood pulled out of the flames: the survivor of the burning of Jerusalem.
b: The image is of a log pulled from a fire just before it is burned up. Amos 4:11 uses it of Israel after a disaster. Here it is Joshua, a survivor of the destruction of 586 whose father Jehozadak was carried away, and also the nation, which has come through the fire of exile. The LORD's argument against the Accuser is not that Joshua is clean, since the next verses show his clothes are filthy, but that the LORD has chosen Jerusalem and has pulled this man out of the fire for a reason. The ground of the pardon in 3:4 is the LORD's own choice (3:2) and not the high priest's record.

p: The Hebrew word for the clothes comes from the word for human waste. The scene is about guilt or uncleanness; what is meant is debated.
b: Tso'im comes from tso'ah, a word for excrement or filth (Isaiah 4:4; Proverbs 30:12), so the clothes are not just dirty, they are disgusting. The garment stands for guilt, which the angel names in 3:4. Whose guilt? The people's: the high priest represents the nation, whose sin brought the exile. The priesthood's: the temple service had been defiled (Malachi 1:6-14 shows later priestly failures). Joshua's own: the Talmud (Sanhedrin 93a) says his sons had married women forbidden to priests. Ritual uncleanness from exile: priests who lived in a foreign land (Amos 7:17; Ezekiel 4:13). The text does not say; it says that the guilt is removed by the LORD (3:4).
r: Isaiah 4:4; Isaiah 64:6; Proverbs 30:12; Amos 7:17; Ezekiel 4:13; Ezra 10:18

a: taken your guilt away from you
p: 'Avon ("guilt") is removed by the LORD, not earned by Joshua. The change of clothes echoes the Day of Atonement.
b: Leviticus 16 has the high priest take off his usual robes and wash on the Day of Atonement, and a goat carries the people's guilt ('avon) away (Leviticus 16:4, 21-22). In Isaiah 6:6-7 a seraph touches the prophet's lips and says his guilt is taken away. Here the guilt is removed and the new clothes are "fine robes" (machalatsot), festal garments. The scene turns the Accuser's charge into a pardon. Later Christian readers found a picture of the forgiveness of sins (Revelation 7:14; Galatians 3:27), and the Reformed and Lutheran traditions in particular read the new robe as a gift from outside the person; see the card on how the churches read it.
r: Leviticus 16:4; Leviticus 16:21-22; Isaiah 6:6-7; Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:9; Revelation 7:14; Galatians 3:27

p: The Hebrew tsanif is a turban worn by kings and, here, by the high priest.
b: The high priest's turban in the law is mitsnefet, with a gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD" (Exodus 28:4, 36-38). Zechariah uses a different word, tsanif, which Isaiah 62:3 uses of a "king's turban" and Job 29:14 of the turban of a just man. So the word may carry a royal tone for the priest, which fits 6:11-13. Zechariah himself steps into the scene with "Then I said," as Amos does in his visions (Amos 7:2, 5). The Greek has no "I said" (see the variant), which would make the order a continuation of the angel's speech.
r: Exodus 28:4; Exodus 28:36-38; Exodus 39:28; Isaiah 62:3; Job 29:14; Zechariah 6:11

a: do the duty I assigned you
p: Mishmeret is the guard duty assigned to priests and Levites.
b: Mishmeret is a technical word for a priestly assignment: the sons of Aaron and the Levites "keep the charge" of the sanctuary (Numbers 3:7-8, 28; Numbers 18:3-5). Ezekiel says the faithful Zadokite priests will "keep my charge" (Ezekiel 44:15-16). Joshua is given the two jobs of the priest: to "govern" (din, which includes judging; Deuteronomy 17:8-12) the house and "guard" the courts. The conditions "if you walk in my ways" repeat the Torah's style (Deuteronomy 8:6). The pardon of 3:4 is a gift, but it comes with a job and a promise of access.

a: let you walk among these who stand here
p: The word is rare. "Those who stand" are probably heavenly attendants, and Joshua is promised a place among them.
b: The noun is mahlekhim, "walkers" or "places to walk," found only here in this form. The Greek has "to walk about among those who stand here." The standing ones are the attendants of the court of 3:1-5, the angels (compare 1 Kings 22:19; Daniel 7:10; Job 1:6). The promise is that the high priest, who had stood as a defendant in a court of angels, will walk among them as one with access. Some commentators read "those who stand" as the priests and so make the promise a reward on earth; the Hebrew allows either.

p: A mofet is a sign or portent. Joshua and his companions are living signs of something coming.
b: Mofet means a portent or wonder; it is used of the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 7:3) and of prophets who are signs, as Ezekiel is a mofet to the exiles (Ezekiel 12:11; Ezekiel 24:24) and Isaiah and his children are "signs and portents" (Isaiah 8:18). So the high priest and the priests who sit with him are a pointer: the thing they stand for has yet to arrive, "my servant, the Branch." Their restored robes foretell something. The crowns of 6:11-14 are another enacted sign of the same kind.

p: Tsemach ("sprout") became a name for the coming Davidic king. Here it points to Zerubbabel, a future king, or both.
b: The word. Tsemach means a sprout. Jeremiah promised "a righteous Branch" for David (Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15). Isaiah 4:2 has "the LORD's branch" (tsemach YHWH), which some read as the produce of the land the LORD blesses and the Targum and much Christian reading take as the Messiah; Isaiah 11:1 a different word for a shoot from Jesse's stump. The Greek translates tsemach as Anatolē, "rising" or "dawn" (here and at 6:12), and Luke 1:78 says that "the Dawn from on high" will visit us. Zerubbabel. The Branch is called "my servant," as Zerubbabel is in Haggai 2:23, and at 6:12-13 he builds the temple, which Zerubbabel does (4:9). His name may even be a pun: Zerubbabel means "offspring of Babylon," and a sprout is "offspring." Many scholars have held that the Branch was Zerubbabel when written; Rose argues against this and reads the Branch as a future royal figure, a new David sent by God. A coming king. Zerubbabel disappears from the record, and the Targum of Zechariah reads "my servant the Messiah" here and at 6:12. Christian readers see Christ. Both: the sign is for Zerubbabel's day and the fuller hope remains open.
r: Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15; Isaiah 4:2; Isaiah 11:1; Haggai 2:23; Zechariah 6:12; Luke 1:78

p: A stone before Joshua has seven "eyes" and is to be engraved; its meaning is disputed.
b: The stone is not named. Views. A foundation or top stone of the Temple (Zechariah 4:7, 10); a jewel on the high priest's turban or breastpiece, since the same verb is used for engraving stones and the gold plate (Exodus 28:9-11, 36); the Messiah as a stone (Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22); a stone with seven facets or springs ("eyes" can mean springs or facets). Seven eyes. The "eyes of the LORD" that roam the earth are seven at 4:10 (and see 2 Chronicles 16:9). In Revelation 5:6 the Lamb has seven horns and seven eyes, "the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth," using the same image. The Dead Sea scroll 4Q80 preserves "seven eyes" here.
r: Zechariah 4:7; Zechariah 4:10; Exodus 28:9-11; Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22; Revelation 5:6

p: The guilt of the whole land is removed in one day, as on the Day of Atonement.
b: Leviticus 16:30 says that on one day the priest makes atonement for the people. Zechariah's "one day" has the same shape: the cleansing of Joshua in the vision is the sign of a day when the land's guilt is removed. The Jewish reading ties it to Yom Kippur and to the end of days. Christian readers have seen the cross, where the author of Hebrews says the high priest's repeated yearly offering is replaced by one offering "once for all" (Hebrews 7:27; Hebrews 9:26-28; Hebrews 10:10). The text itself gives no date.
r: Leviticus 16:30; Hebrews 7:27; Hebrews 9:26-28; Hebrews 10:10; Zechariah 13:1; Zechariah 14:9

a: under a vine and under a fig tree
p: The old picture of peace under Solomon, now a promise.
b: First Kings 4:25 says that in Solomon's days Judah and Israel lived "each under his own vine and his own fig tree." Micah 4:4 promises the same for the future, and 2 Kings 18:31 and Isaiah 36:16 use it for what Assyria offered a surrendering city. Zechariah's twist is the invitation: each person will invite a neighbor to come and sit under the vine. Peace is shared, and a mark of it is hospitality. Compare 8:4-5 and 8:21-23, where the peace of the city draws others in.

p: The angel wakes the prophet "like a man woken from sleep"; the visions are experienced at night.
b: The visions come in one night (1:8) and the prophet is woken from a state like sleep before the fifth. It is not a dream in the ordinary sense, since he sees with his eyes and answers, but a trance-like state between sleeping and waking; Daniel is overcome and then roused by an angel's touch (Daniel 8:18; Daniel 10:9). This is the only waking in the series; the visions after it begin with the prophet turning and lifting his eyes again (5:1; 6:1).

a: a lampstand made entirely of gold
p: Like the Tabernacle's menorah, but with a bowl on top and pipes: a lamp that is fed without a priest.
b: The Tabernacle's lampstand had seven lamps on a stem with six branches (Exodus 25:31-40), and Solomon's temple had ten (1 Kings 7:49). This one has a bowl or reservoir on top, seven lamps and pipes to the lamps, and two olive trees beside it. The trees supply the oil directly, so no priest has to fill the lamps (4:12). The image shows light that never runs out because the supply is the LORD's own. In Revelation the seven lampstands are the seven churches (Revelation 1:12, 20) and the two lampstands the two witnesses (Revelation 11:4), which draw from this chapter. The seven lamps match the seven eyes of 4:10.
r: Exodus 25:31-40; 1 Kings 7:49; Revelation 1:12; Revelation 1:20; Revelation 11:4; Zechariah 4:10

p: "Seven and seven pipes" can mean seven in all, fourteen, or seven to each of the seven lamps (forty-nine).
b: The Hebrew is shiv'ah ushiv'ah mutsaqot, "seven and seven pipes." Seven in all, one for each lamp (the repeating "seven and seven" is a way of saying "seven each"). Fourteen, two for each lamp. Forty-nine, seven for each of the seven lamps. The Greek reads "seven lamps ... and seven pourers," which supports the first view. The count does not change the sense: a lavish supply of oil.

p: Two trees feed the lampstand with oil; 4:14 calls them "the two sons of fresh oil."
b: The trees stand to the right and left of the bowl and are the source of its oil. The key is 4:14: they are "the two sons of fresh oil who stand by the Lord of the whole earth." Most scholars say they are Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, the two leaders. The book gives that reading no direct word, but the roles of the two men in Haggai and Zechariah and their joint appearance (6:13) fit it. The olive tree is a sign of life and blessing (Psalm 52:8; Psalm 128:3; Jeremiah 11:16; Romans 11:17-24).
r: Psalm 52:8; Psalm 128:3; Jeremiah 11:16; Romans 11:17; Revelation 11:4; Zechariah 4:14

a: Not by strength and not by force, but by my Spirit
t: "Not by might": a slogan and its context
p: The Temple will not be built by an army or force but by the LORD's Spirit. Often used as a slogan; the context is narrower.
b: Chayil is strength, wealth, or an army (Exodus 14:4, where it is Pharaoh's army); koach is power, force. "Spirit" is ruach (the Plain capitalizes it where it is the LORD's own, as in Joel 2:28). The common misreading turns the verse into a rule that human effort is useless. It is not: the next verses say Zerubbabel's own hands "founded this house, and his hands will bring it to completion" (4:9). The setting. A few years earlier the Persian throne had been shaken by revolts, and some may have hoped that Zerubbabel, a descendant of David, would lead one. On one common reading, the word to him is that the Temple will come through the LORD's work and not through arms, with the Persian government's consent (Ezra 6:6-12). The Spirit is also the one who sent the earlier prophets' words (7:12) and who stands among the builders (Haggai 2:5).
orig: לֹא בְחַיִל וְלֹא בְכֹחַ כִּי אִם־בְּרוּחִי (lo vechayil velo vekoach ki im beruchi)
r: Haggai 2:5; Zechariah 7:12; Joel 2:28; Isaiah 11:2; Isaiah 63:10-14; Ezekiel 36:27

p: A mountain that becomes a plain before Zerubbabel: the obstacles in the way of the Temple.
b: The mountain stands for whatever blocks the builders. Ezra 4-5 lists the obstacles: the opposition of the neighbors, the order to stop and Tattenai's inquiry. Others have read it as the heap of ruins on the old Temple mount, or as Babylon, called a "destroying mountain" in Jeremiah 51:25, or as the whole empire. The same image is used for removing impossible obstacles in Isaiah 40:4, where mountains are made level, and in Jesus' saying about moving a mountain by faith (Matthew 17:20; Matthew 21:21). The "level ground" (mishor) is a flat plain on which a building can be built. The Greek adds "to make straight" (katorthōsai).
r: Ezra 4:4-5; Ezra 5:3; Isaiah 40:4; Jeremiah 51:25; Matthew 17:20; Matthew 21:21

p: Ezra puts a foundation under Cyrus; Haggai and Zechariah put one in 520. The sources are read in different ways.
b: Ezra 3:8-13 describes a foundation laid under Zerubbabel and Jeshua soon after the return, with weeping and shouting; Ezra 5:16 quotes the Persian officials as reporting that Sheshbazzar laid the foundation; Haggai 2:18 dates "the day the LORD's temple was founded" to 24 Kislev (18 December) 520. Zechariah says Zerubbabel's hands laid the foundation and will finish it (4:9) and, in 8:9, refers to the day the foundation was laid. Views. A first foundation in 537-536 followed by a stoppage and a ceremony in 520; a foundation by Sheshbazzar and a rededication by Zerubbabel; or a single event in 520 that Ezra 3 has moved earlier. The book of Zechariah is the contemporary source and makes Zerubbabel the builder. The promised completion came in March 515 (Ezra 6:15).

a: Then you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me to you
p: The line appears four times (2:9, 2:11, 4:9, 6:15): the proof of the prophet is that the Temple will be finished.
b: Deuteronomy 18:21-22 gave the test of a true prophet: if his word comes true, the LORD sent him. Zechariah uses the formula for a test that can be checked: "his hands will bring it to completion." The Temple was finished on the third of Adar in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15), about 516-515 BC, three or four years after this vision. The same formula in 2:9, 2:11 and 6:15 ties each promise to the prophet's credibility. As in 2:8, the speaker who says "the LORD has sent me" is the angel or the prophet; the Hebrew does not say.

a: a day when things were small
p: A line for discouraged builders. In Zechariah it answers the grief that the new Temple looked like nothing.
b: Haggai had asked the old people who had seen Solomon's Temple, "Is it not like nothing in your eyes?" (Haggai 2:3), and Ezra 3:12-13 says the old men wept when they saw the new foundation. Zechariah answers: the LORD does not look down on small things, and the builders will rejoice. The line is often quoted today for small beginnings in general; here it speaks of one project, the second Temple. The saying matches 1 Corinthians 1:27-28, though Paul does not cite it.

p: A stone of tin or lead in Zerubbabel's hand is probably a plumb weight, showing the work is straight.
b: Ha'even habbedil is literally "the tin stone." Bedil is tin (Numbers 31:22; Ezekiel 22:18). A plumb line hangs a metal weight to check that a wall is vertical, and the seven eyes watching the measurement suggest an inspection. Alternatives: a stone for a sacred purpose, the top stone of 4:7 given a new name, or a stone of tin in the sense of a piece of the foundation ceremony. The Greek reads "the tin stone" without comment. Whatever the object, it is in Zerubbabel's hand and the LORD's eyes are on it.

a: These seven are the LORD's eyes
p: The LORD's eyes are the lamps; the Persian king had officials called his eyes.
b: The seven lamps of 4:2 are the seven eyes of the LORD that "roam over all the earth," the same figure as 2 Chronicles 16:9. The image says that God is the world's ruler and sees. Xenophon writes that the Persian king had "king's eyes" and "king's ears" (Cyropaedia 8.2.10). The seven eyes of the stone in 3:9 are the same. In Revelation the Lamb has seven eyes, "the seven spirits of God" (Revelation 5:6), and the seven lamps of fire before the throne are the seven spirits (Revelation 4:5); the link is by image, not by quotation.

p: "Gold" here is probably golden oil; the Hebrew simply says "gold."
b: The scene is odd: the olive branches empty "the gold" through two gold spouts into the bowl. Most commentators take the gold as the golden oil, the oil that gleams. Another view takes it as a metonymy for the bowl's contents. The Plain keeps the Hebrew's "gold" without adding the word oil. The Greek "pourers" (epaarystrides) and "spouts" (muxōtēras) are its own renderings.

a: the two sons of fresh oil
t: The two sons of fresh oil
p: Not "anointed ones": the Hebrew says "sons of fresh oil." Who they are is the key to the chapter.
b: Yitshar is freshly pressed oil, not the shemen used for anointing, and the word mashiach ("anointed") does not occur, so the common English "anointed ones" adds to the Hebrew. Views. Zerubbabel and Joshua, the king and priest (most commentators; the roles are those of the two leaders and anointed offices). Haggai and Zechariah, the two prophets. In Revelation 11:3-4 the two witnesses are called "the two olive trees and the two lampstands," a transformation of this image, not an identification.

p: A scroll as big as the Temple's porch, carrying a curse over the land. The Greek reads "sickle."
b: The scroll is twenty cubits by ten (about 30 by 15 feet, or 9 by 4.5 meters), the size of the Holy Place in the Tabernacle and of the porch of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6:3). A scroll that big is a public notice, written large and flying so it can be seen everywhere. It carries a curse like the curses "written in this scroll" in Deuteronomy 29:20-21, and like Ezekiel's scroll of laments, sighing and woe (Ezekiel 2:9-10). In Revelation the angel's little scroll (Revelation 10:2, 8-11) and the sealed scroll (Revelation 5:1) are related images. The Greek has drepanon, "sickle," at 5:1-2 (see the variant). Some read the size as a sign that the curse is the Torah itself, a law that covers the whole land.

a: twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide
p: A cubit is about 18 inches (45 centimeters), so the scroll is about 30 by 15 feet.
b: The cubit was the distance from the elbow to the fingertip, about 18 inches or 45 centimeters. Twenty by ten cubits matches the Tabernacle's Holy Place (Exodus 26) and Solomon's Temple porch (1 Kings 6:3). The match may be accidental, or it may suggest that the curse goes out from the sanctuary's standard to the whole land: the law of the Temple governs the land. The Greek has the same measurements for its "sickle."

p: 'Alah is the oath-curse of a covenant. It falls on two crimes, one against a neighbor and one against God.
b: 'Alah is the curse-oath that goes with a covenant. Deuteronomy 29:12, 19-21 speaks of "the oath and the curse" on those who break the covenant. The two crimes named are stealing and swearing falsely: one is about a neighbor's property (the eighth commandment) and the other about the LORD's name (the third commandment). Commentators often see them as a sample of both sides of the Ten Commandments, one for each side of the scroll. The curse is a legal process: it is sent out (5:4) and arrives at a house.

p: The verb niqqah can mean be cleared out, be punished, or be acquitted; commentators differ.
b: Naqah means to be clean or clear. In the passive it can mean "to be emptied out, swept away" (the usual view here), or "to be cleared of guilt, to go unpunished" (as in Exodus 20:7, where the same verb in the negative says the LORD will not leave unpunished one who takes his name for something empty). Here it falls on the thief and the false swearer, so it is the curse's action: they are swept away. The Greek says they will be "punished until death." The Plain keeps a neutral picture, "swept away," which reads as a clearing of the land. A few take the verb as ironic or as an acquittal until the curse hits.

a: stay inside that house and destroy it
t: The curse that lodges in a house
p: The curse stays all night and consumes the house, as a mold-infested house in the law had to be torn down.
b: The verb lun means to stay the night. The curse lodges in the house like a visitor who will not leave. The law of skin disease in a house required tearing it down, "its stones, its timbers and all its plaster" (Leviticus 14:45), when it could not be cleaned. Zechariah's curse takes "its timbers and its stones" in the same way. The picture is that dishonest wealth does not last: wood and stone, the signs of a prosperous house, are the first things the curse takes (compare Habakkuk 2:9-11).

a: the ephah that is going out
p: An ephah is a dry measure of about 22 liters (two thirds of a bushel); dishonest ephahs are a theme of the prophets.
b: The ephah is a standard measure of grain, a tenth of a homer (Ezekiel 45:11; Ezekiel 45:13-14). Exodus 16:36 gives the related measure the other way round: the omer is a tenth of an ephah. It is also the object most often cheated: Amos speaks of those who "make the ephah small" (Amos 8:5) and Micah condemns "the short ephah" (Micah 6:10-11). Leviticus 19:35-36 and Deuteronomy 25:13-16 require honest measures. So an ephah in a vision of crimes against neighbors points to commerce, where theft and false oaths happen. The ephah in the vision is large enough to hold a woman, so it is not an ordinary one. The Greek calls it metron, "a measure."
r: Exodus 16:36; Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-16; Amos 8:5; Micah 6:10-11; Ezekiel 45:10-11

p: Kikkar is a round disk, or a talent-weight; the lid is lead, a heavy and cheap metal.
b: Kikkar means a round thing: a flat loaf (Exodus 29:23), a district (the "plain" of the Jordan), a "talent" (a large weight; 1 Kings 9:14). The Greek reads "a talent of lead," a lead weight. Oferet is lead (Numbers 31:22; Jeremiah 6:29). The lid is raised so the prophet can see the woman, then pushed down with the lead weight at 5:8. The detail stresses that she cannot get out.

p: Rish'ah is a feminine noun; the woman is evil itself, carried to Shinar. What that means is disputed.
b: Rish'ah ("wickedness") is feminine in Hebrew, as most abstract nouns are. Views: (a) the land's sins taken out and sent away, as 3:9 and 5:3-4 treat sin as something removed (compare the scapegoat, Leviticus 16:21-22); (b) a goddess or idol, a foreign cult figure packed up and returned to Babylon, where she belongs (so some scholars, citing the shrine she is given); (c) social crimes of dishonest commerce (the ephah) or of the community of Yehud. Some modern readers object that evil is made a woman, and respond that the grammar is why (Wisdom and Folly are both women in Proverbs). Revelation 17 and 18 place a woman called "Babylon" at the end, but the two scenes are not the same.

p: The stork (chasidah, "the loyal one") is an unclean bird; the women who carry Wickedness have its wings.
b: Chasidah is probably the white stork, a bird that migrates in large flocks and is named in Jeremiah 8:7 and Psalm 104:17. The name comes from hesed ("loyal love"), perhaps because storks care for their young. It is listed among the unclean birds in Leviticus 11:19 and Deuteronomy 14:18. So the bearers of Wickedness are unclean, and they are carried by "wind in their wings," wind that does the carrying. The women are unnamed; they are not described as good or evil. The topic on the ephah woman sets out the views.

p: The old name for Babylonia, tied to the Tower of Babel; a house is built there for Wickedness.
b: Shinar (Shin'ar) is the Bible's old name for the plain of Babylonia, the land of Nimrod's kingdom (Genesis 10:10) and of the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:2). In Isaiah 11:11 and Daniel 1:2 it is where captives went. Zechariah uses it for Babylon, which the Greek translates as "the land of Babylon." The "house" built there with a "base" is a shrine: Wickedness will have her own temple, set up in the country that stands for human pride, while the true Temple is built in Jerusalem (4:9). Some see here a final exile of evil from the land, others a judgment on Babylon, which will receive what it practiced.

p: The chariots come out of two bronze mountains; the text does not say what they are.
b: Suggestions: the two bronze pillars at the Temple's entrance, Jachin and Boaz (1 Kings 7:15-22); Mount Zion and the Mount of Olives, one on each side of the valley; the gates of the heavenly dwelling of the LORD, as the "Lord of all the earth" (6:5) has an entrance. Bronze is strong and polished and shines in sunlight. The vision answers the first vision (1:8-11) in which horses stand in a hollow; the chariots here are sent out by the LORD, not returning from a patrol. The text gives no key.

p: The fourth team is "dappled, strong"; many think "strong" (amutsim) replaces "red."
b: The chariots have red, black, white and dappled horses (6:2-3). In 6:6 the black, white and dappled teams are sent out, and 6:7 sends "the strong" ones, with no red team mentioned. Many commentators think the word amutsim ("strong") in 6:3 and 6:7 is an old scribal slip for adummim ("red"). The Greek calls the fourth team "dappled and gray" (poikiloi psaroi). The Plain keeps the Hebrew as it stands.

a: the four winds of the heavens
p: Ruchot can mean winds or spirits. The four teams are heavenly forces sent from the LORD's court.
b: Ruach is wind, breath or spirit, and the plural can be either. The Greek has "winds." The Hebrew of 2:6 also says "four winds of the heavens." In Psalm 104:4 the LORD "makes winds his messengers," and in Revelation 7:1 four angels hold the four winds of the earth. So the four teams are the LORD's agents going to the four corners of the earth, and the reading "spirits" gives them the same standing as angels. They come "after standing before the Lord of all the earth," like the courtiers in Job 1:6.

p: The north is Babylon, the old direction of invasion; the south is Egypt. The east and west are not named.
b: "The land of the north" is where Israel's enemies entered (Jeremiah 1:14; Jeremiah 6:22) and where the exiles were carried (2:6). Babylon lies east of Judah but a traveler had to go north along the road around the desert, so Hebrew calls it "north." The south is probably Egypt, which Persia held. The east and the west are not mentioned, and the first team (red) is missing from 6:6 (see 6:3). The black team, sent north, has the main task (6:8).

p: The Hebrew ruchi can be "my Spirit" or "my anger"; the Greek chooses anger.
b: The verb heniach means to give rest. The noun ruach can be wind, spirit, or temper: in Judges 8:3 "their anger (ruach) toward him subsided," and the Greek of this verse has thymon mou, "my anger." If it is anger, the north is Babylon, and the LORD's wrath against it is satisfied (compare 1:15 and 2:8-9). If it is the Spirit, the LORD's Spirit has been given rest in the north, just as Isaiah 63:14 says the Spirit gave Israel rest (tenichennu). The Plain says "my spirit" in lower case and leaves the question open.

p: Three men from the Babylonian Jews have come with gifts for the Temple; the prophet is sent to them.
b: Heldai, Tobiah and Jedaiah are a group of men who have just arrived from Babylon with silver and gold for the Temple (6:11). The prophet is told to go on the same day to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, where they are staying. It is evidence of support from the Babylonian Jewish communities: other gifts in Ezra 1:6 and Ezra 8:25-34. The Hebrew sentence is awkward, and "who came from Babylon" may describe the three men or Josiah. The names are discussed in the variants (6:10; 6:14).

p: The Hebrew 'atarot is plural. It may be one grand crown, two crowns, or a sign of a text that was changed.
b: 'Atarah is a crown, usually a king's (2 Samuel 12:30; Esther 8:15; Psalm 21:3). The plural can be a plural of grandeur, one crown of several bands (compare Job 31:36 and Revelation 19:12, "many crowns"); two crowns, one for Joshua and one for Zerubbabel (6:13 speaks of "the two of them"); or the result of editing. The editing view (held by some critical scholars): the original said Zerubbabel was crowned, and a later hand changed it to Joshua after Zerubbabel disappeared from history, or because the Persians would not allow a Davidic king. The reading as it stands: Joshua is crowned as a sign (3:8), pointing to another, "a man whose name is Branch" (6:12). The Greek has "crowns" in the plural, too.
r: 2 Samuel 12:30; Esther 8:15; Psalm 21:3; Revelation 19:12; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:13

a: Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest
p: Joshua is crowned, but the oracle that follows is about another man. How the two fit is debated.
b: As written. Joshua receives a crown as a symbolic act (like Ezekiel 4-5), and the crown stands for the future Branch, who will be both priest and king (6:12-13). The Branch is spoken of in the third person, so the man crowned is not the Branch. Zerubbabel dropped out. Critical scholars see an earlier text in which Zerubbabel was crowned, and a revision after he vanished. A priestly leader. Others see here the beginning of a priest-led community under Persian rule, which led later to the Hasmonean priest-kings (1 Maccabees 14:41-47). Jewish and Christian readers: the Targum reads the Branch as the Messiah; the Christian reading takes him as Christ, priest and king (Hebrews 5:5-10; Hebrews 7). See the card on the priest-king.

a: From his own place he will branch out
p: The verb is from the same root as the name: tsemach ... yitsmach.
b: "Branch" and "will branch out" are tsemach and yitsmach. The Plain keeps the pun. The Hebrew says "from under him" (mittachtav), which means from his own place or from his own roots, as when a plant sprouts at its own base. The Greek makes the name Anatolē ("Dawn") and the verb "will rise." See the note on the Branch at 3:8 for the identifications. The Branch "builds the temple of the LORD," a job Zerubbabel has already begun (4:9). Jewish tradition gave the Messiah the task of building the Temple (Maimonides, Laws of Kings 11:1).

a: He will also be a priest on that throne
t: Priest and king: one person or two?
p: The Hebrew puts a priest "on his throne" with peace between the two. The Greek has the priest "at his right."
b: One person: the Branch is both king and priest, and "the two of them" are the two offices (so many Jewish and Christian readers; Psalm 110:1, 4 joins sitting at the LORD's right hand with being a priest forever). Two persons: a king and a priest each on his own throne, in harmony, like Zerubbabel and Joshua (the Greek says "the priest will be at his right"; the Dead Sea Scrolls expect a royal and a priestly messiah). A text change: an original about two men that was edited. The Plain follows the Hebrew words. The word "throne" for a priest is unusual: the law gave priests no throne. The churches that name the Branch here agree: the Catholic Catechism (436) and the Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 31) both speak of Christ as prophet, priest and king, and Calvin reads 6:12-13 of Christ, whom the Father chose to build the temple. The disagreement is between that reading and the Jewish and critical ones above, so there is no traditions card.

p: People "far away" will come and build the Temple: exiles still in Babylon, or foreign nations.
b: Rechokim ("far ones") can mean Jews still abroad, as the delegation from Babylon (6:10) has come from far; or non-Jews who will help to build, as in Isaiah 60:10 and Haggai 2:7. Isaiah 57:19 speaks of peace to "the far and the near." Christian readers find here the Gentiles joining God's people; Paul says that Gentiles who were "far off" have been brought near (Ephesians 2:13, 17), and Peter says the promise is for "all those far away" (Acts 2:39). The Jewish and Christian readings differ over whether the temple of the end is a building or the community; see the note at 8:23.
r: Isaiah 57:19; Isaiah 60:10; Haggai 2:7; Acts 2:39; Ephesians 2:13; Zechariah 2:11; Zechariah 8:20-23

p: The sentence stops after "if you really listen" and gives no result.
b: The Hebrew is shamoa tishme'un, "if you listen, you listen," the emphatic plural form of Exodus 19:5 (Deuteronomy 28:1 opens with the same words in the singular). In both places the next words are the blessings. Here the sentence ends, so the reader must supply the promise. Some see a deliberate silence, others a damaged text. The effect is that the prophecy of the Branch, the crowns and the far-off builders is a promise on condition of obedience, as the whole book says (1:3-6; 7:11-14).

p: The fasting question comes 22 months after the night visions and about three years before the Temple was finished.
b: The fourth day of the ninth month (Kislev) of Darius's fourth year converts to 7 December 518 BC by the usual conversion. It is two years after Haggai's 18 December 520, when the foundation was laid (Haggai 2:18), and almost two years after the visions (1:7). The Temple would be finished in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15). The book now moves from visions to a question and a long answer, in prose, with no angel. The fasts in question mark events of 586 (2 Kings 25:8, 25; Jeremiah 41:1-3).

p: The Hebrew idiom is "to soften the LORD's face" (chalah panim). It returns at 8:21-22.
b: Chalah et-penei YHWH is literally "to make soft the face of the LORD": to plead, to try to get his favor (Exodus 32:11; 1 Kings 13:6; Malachi 1:9). In 7:2 a small delegation is sent to do it. In 8:21-22 whole cities and nations go up to Jerusalem to do the same. The inclusion is the book's answer: a question from a village in Benjamin becomes an invitation to the world.

p: Bethel, a town north of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, sends two men with a question.
b: Bethel was in Benjamin and was resettled after the exile (Ezra 2:28; Nehemiah 7:32). It had been a royal shrine of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:29-33; Amos 7:13), and Jeremiah 41:5 shows worshipers from the north coming to the ruined Temple. The delegation's names are Sharezer, from an Akkadian name meaning "protect the king" (compare 2 Kings 19:37), and Regem-melech, a name whose meaning is debated ("friend of the king" is a common guess). The Hebrew can be read "Bethel sent Sharezer and Regem-melech" (as the Plain has it), "Bethel-sharezer and Regem-melech sent men," or "the house of God sent." The Hebrew ends "and his men" (va'anashav), which the Plain keeps as "his men." The Greek understands the verse as "he sent to Bethel" (see the variant).

a: Am I to go on weeping in the fifth month and keeping myself apart
t: The question: should the fast go on?
p: Now that the Temple is being rebuilt, should the community go on mourning its destruction?
b: The fifth month (Av) was the month the Temple burned (2 Kings 25:8-9; Jeremiah 52:12-13). The people fasted and "kept apart" (nazar, "to separate oneself" from food and pleasure) for seventy years. With the new Temple under construction, they ask the priests and prophets whether the mourning should continue. The speaker "I" is the community. Only the fifth month is named in the question; the answer widens it to the seventh (7:5) and to four fasts (8:19). The Greek gives the verse a different meaning (see the variant).

a: Did you really fast for me, for me?
p: The LORD's answer to the fast question is a question: were you fasting for me, or for yourselves?
b: The Hebrew puts the verb twice, "fasting, did you fast for me, for me?", for emphasis. The question runs through the prophets: ritual that is not tied to justice is empty. Isaiah 58:3-7 has the people ask why God does not see their fast, and the answer is that he wants release of the oppressed, bread for the hungry and shelter. Joel 2:12-13 asks for torn hearts and not torn clothes, and Jesus says that fasting is not to be done for show (Matthew 6:16-18). Zechariah does not say fasting is wrong; he says it must be for the LORD. The answer in 7:9-10 and 8:16-17 is the ethical one.

p: Here "the people of the land" are ordinary citizens of Judah, with the priests: the whole community.
b: 'Am ha'arets means different things in different books. In 2 Kings 11:14 and 21:24 it is the landowning citizens who act politically. In Ezra 4:4 and 10:2 it is a hostile term for people who opposed the returned exiles, and in Haggai 2:4 it is the whole community of Judah, which is the sense here. In Zechariah 7:5 it appears with the priests: laity and clergy together. The topic on the people of the land follows the changing use.

a: are you not the ones who eat and the ones who drink?
p: Eating is self-directed too: the feasts were no better than the fasts, or the fasts no different from meals.
b: The LORD's rhetorical question can be read two ways. Both were for yourselves: as the fasts were not for me, the meals and feasts that came after were not either; neither fasting nor feasting was directed at God. No difference: the fasts were as ordinary as meals, since they produced no change in life. The sense is the same: religious acts done only for oneself. The Greek ("do you not eat and drink?") leaves out the pronoun "you."

p: Before 586 Judah included the Negev (south) and the Shephelah (west); under Persia, Yehud was much smaller.
b: The Negev is the dry southern region around Beersheba; the Shephelah is the fertile foothill country west of the hill country, with towns such as Lachish and Azekah. Before 586 both were Judean. In the Persian period the province of Yehud was a much smaller area around Jerusalem, and Edomites had moved into the southern land (Idumea). So the verse sets today's small province beside the settled kingdom of the earlier prophets. The Hebrew sentence ("Are these not the words ...") has no verb; the Plain does not add one.

t: True justice, loyal love and compassion
p: Three words from the law: true justice, hesed and compassion, put in the form of a command to each person.
b: Mishpat emet is "justice of truth": judgment that matches the facts, as in Ezekiel 18:8. Hesed ("loyal love") and rachamim ("compassion") are the two words of the LORD's own character in Exodus 34:6 and Micah 6:8. The prophets joined them in a single demand: Hosea 12:6, Micah 6:8 and Jeremiah 22:3 are close. Here the audience is the ordinary people, not only the judges: "each to his brother." The Plain keeps "justice" for mishpat and "truth" for emet throughout the book.
r: Exodus 34:6; Hosea 12:6; Micah 6:8; Jeremiah 22:3; Ezekiel 18:8; Zechariah 8:16

a: the foreigner who lives among you
p: Widow, fatherless, foreigner and poor are the people the law protects.
b: The list is a standard one: the widow, the fatherless child and the resident foreigner (ger) in Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17-21 and 27:19; in Jeremiah 7:6 and 22:3 and Ezekiel 22:7, with the poor added in Zechariah. The Plain's "foreigner who lives among you" is the term for ger. The prophets say a community is judged by how it treats these four. Zechariah's addition, the ban on planning harm "in your hearts," moves from deeds to thoughts, as in Deuteronomy 15:9.

p: Nehemiah 9:29 has the same words. The picture is an ox that will not take the yoke.
b: Katef sorerret is "a rebellious shoulder," an animal pulling away from its yoke (Hosea 4:16, "a stubborn heifer"). The Plain follows Nehemiah 9:29 ("They gave you a defiant shoulder"). The combination of the defiant shoulder, the heavy ears and the flint heart (7:12) is Zechariah's summary of the exile's cause. The same list returns in Stephen's speech, "Stiff-necked men, uncircumcised in your hearts and in your ears!" (Acts 7:51).

p: The earlier prophets spoke by the LORD's Spirit; Nehemiah 9:30 says the same.
b: The sentence says the LORD sent "the law and the words" "by his Spirit through the earlier prophets." Nehemiah 9:30 has the same pairing of Spirit and prophets. For Zechariah, the prophets did not speak on their own: the Spirit was behind them, and the Spirit is also with the builders (4:6; Haggai 2:5). "The law" is torah, the teaching; the prophets and the law are put together as one message. In the New Testament, 2 Peter 1:21 says prophets spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

a: When he called, they would not listen
p: The LORD's refusal to answer matches the people's refusal to listen.
b: The pattern of "I called and you would not listen; you will call and I will not answer" is found in Proverbs 1:24-28 and Jeremiah 11:11 ("They will cry out to me, and I will not listen to them"). Isaiah 1:15 and Micah 3:4 are close. Who "called" at the start is not stated: the LORD, or the prophets in his name. The sentence is a harsh one, and it is placed in the past: the exile is the day the LORD did not answer. The book's next section (chapter 8) says that day is over.

p: The "pleasant land" of the covenant is what was turned into a waste.
b: Eretz chemdah is "a desirable land." Jeremiah 3:19 uses the phrase for the inheritance God wanted to give, and Psalm 106:24 says the people "despised the pleasant land." Zechariah says they "turned" it into a waste, so the destruction is tied to their action. A se'arah is a storm or whirlwind (Isaiah 29:6; Ezekiel 1:4), here the exile: the LORD blew them among nations they did not know (Deuteronomy 28:64).

p: 'Emet, "truth," means firmness and reliability; the city will be called by it.
b: 'Emet is truth in the sense of what holds up. The Plain uses "truth" every time (7:9 "true justice"; 8:3; 8:8; 8:16; 8:19). Isaiah 1:21, 26 calls Jerusalem a faithful city that became a prostitute and then will be called "the city of righteousness, the faithful city." Ezekiel 48:35 gives the new city the name "The LORD Is There." The Greek has polis hē alēthinē, "the true city." The promise is a character: the city will be what it should be. "I have returned to Zion" (8:3) answers the departure of the glory in Ezekiel 10-11 and the call to return in 1:3.

a: Once more old men and old women will sit in Jerusalem's squares
t: Old and young in the streets
p: A picture of the city's safety: the old sit, the children play. It reverses the city of Lamentations.
b: Lamentations describes the opposite: children and infants faint in the city squares (Lamentations 2:11-12, 19), and the elders have left the gate (Lamentations 5:14). Zechariah adds old men with staffs and children at play in the squares, with every age present and secure. A long life is a covenant blessing (Isaiah 65:20-22). The squares (rechovot) are the open spaces of the city where people met and where the nation had once stood to hear Ezra (Nehemiah 8:1).

p: The same verb as Genesis 18:14: is anything too wonderful, or too hard, for the LORD?
b: Yipale is from pala, "to be wonderful, extraordinary, too hard." It is the word asked of Sarah's laughter, "Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?" (Genesis 18:14), and of Jeremiah 32:17, 27, "nothing is too hard for you." The Plain follows the Genesis wording. Here the remnant finds the promise too good to believe; the LORD asks if it is too good for him. "The remnant of this people" is the community under Zerubbabel and Joshua, whom Haggai called by the same name (Haggai 1:12-14).

a: the land of the east and from the land of the setting sun
p: By 518 Jews lived in Babylon, Egypt and elsewhere; the promise reaches them all.
b: The exile created communities in Babylonia (Ezekiel 1:1; Ezra 2), in Egypt (Jeremiah 43-44), and others. A Jewish military colony at Elephantine on the Nile is known from papyri of the fifth century BC. "East and west" is a way of saying everywhere (Psalm 107:3; Isaiah 43:5-6; Malachi 1:11). The promise to bring them back to Jerusalem was only partly kept in the Persian period. Jewish tradition has read it as the ingathering of exiles, which every Jewish prayer book still asks for, and Christian readers have often seen the gathering of Jews and Gentiles into the church (John 11:52).

a: They will be my people, and I will be their God
p: The oldest covenant sentence in the Bible, said here of the returning exiles.
b: "I will be your God and you will be my people" is the covenant formula (Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12). It returns in Jeremiah 24:7; 30:22; 31:33; 32:38 and Ezekiel 11:20; 36:28; 37:27, each time at a restoration. Zechariah adds "in truth and in righteousness." The New Testament uses the formula for the church: 2 Corinthians 6:16, Hebrews 8:10 and Revelation 21:3. In Zechariah the same sentence is used of the nations at 2:11, so the formula is already stretched.
r: Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27; Zechariah 2:11; Hebrews 8:10; Revelation 21:3

a: the day the LORD of Armies' house was founded
p: "The prophets" who spoke on the founding day are Haggai and Zechariah; the day is probably 24 Kislev 520.
b: The prophets who spoke "on the day the foundation was laid" are Haggai and Zechariah (Ezra 5:1-2). Haggai 2:18 dates the founding day to the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, 18 December 520, and Zechariah's message here is dated in the same month two years later. The writer of 8:9 is looking back to that day. See the note on 4:9 for the debate over which foundation is meant. The effect is to ask the people to hold on to what was said then: the work is not finished.

a: people earned no pay and animals brought in nothing
p: A look back at the poverty of 520 and before: no pay, no safety, and neighbor against neighbor.
