b: The picture matches Haggai 1:6, 9-11 and 2:16-17: little income, empty barns and a drought. The Hebrew says there was no wage for a person or an animal, no safety for anyone coming or going, and the LORD set every person against his neighbor. The last phrase says that the conflict inside the community was part of the judgment. Nehemiah 5 shows what such conflict looked like later: loans, debts and the selling of children.

a: Seed will be sown in peace
p: Zera hashalom is hard: peaceful sowing, a sowing of peace, or seed that will thrive.
b: The Hebrew is literally "the seed of peace." Readings: the seed will be sown in peace (the Plain), the seed will thrive (as in the older English "the seed shall be prosperous"), there will be a sowing of peace, or a small change to the text, "the seed will be sown" (some commentators). Whatever the reading, the verse reverses Haggai's drought: the vine, the land and "the heavens will give their dew" (Haggai 1:10 says the heavens held back dew). The land that was cursed (Haggai 1:11) is blessed. "Inheritance" is the word of Joshua 1:6 and shows that the land is given by the LORD.

a: were a curse among the nations
t: From a curse to a blessing
p: Judah had become a word used in curses; now it is to be used in blessings, as Abraham was promised.
b: To be "a curse" is to be a byword: people said "May you end like Judah" when they cursed (compare Jeremiah 29:22, where exiles curse by the names of Zedekiah and Ahab). The reversal, "you will be a blessing," takes up the promise to Abraham to be a blessing (Genesis 12:2), so that all the clans of the earth find blessing in him (Genesis 12:3). Both the house of Judah and the house of Israel are named, so the promise covers the north as well, as in Jeremiah 31:31 and Ezekiel 37:15-23. The two houses were once separate kingdoms.

a: I did not change my mind
p: The same root as "comfort" in 1:13. The LORD did not change his mind about the harm; now he has turned to good.
b: Nacham of God in the "change one's mind" sense, as in Jeremiah 18:8, 10 and 26:3, is rendered "change his mind" in the Plain; the negative form is in Jeremiah 4:28 ("I have not changed my mind"). Zechariah says the LORD did not hold back the harm he planned (zamam) when their ancestors provoked him, and now plans (zamam again) to do good. The same root in the other stem is "comfort" (1:13, 17), which ties the book together. The verse gives the theological balance: the LORD's judgment in the past was not reversed by the people's complaint, but his word to them now is not reversed either (8:15). See the topic on God's regret.
r: Jeremiah 4:28; Jeremiah 18:8; Jeremiah 26:3; Zechariah 1:6; Zechariah 1:13; Zechariah 1:17

a: judge with truth and with justice that makes for peace
p: Courts met in the city gate; the command is to the elders who sat there.
b: In ancient Israel the elders sat at the city gate to judge (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1-2; Amos 5:12, 15). "Truth, and justice that makes for peace" (mishpat shalom) means a verdict that ends the quarrel and not just wins it. The first half of the verse, "Speak truth, each of you to your neighbor," is quoted by Paul in Ephesians 4:25 in its Greek form. The commands match 7:9-10 and form a frame around the long answer on fasting.

a: Do not plan harm against one another in your hearts
p: The commands of 7:9-10 return word for word here, closing the answer where it opened.
b: Zechariah 7:9-10 and 8:16-17 give nearly the same list: true justice, loyal love, no planning harm in the heart. The repetition frames the whole of 7:8 to 8:17, and shows what the "fast for me" of 7:5 should have been. "A false oath" ties back to the flying scroll (5:3-4), which fell on the one "who swears falsely by my name." It also stands against the third commandment (Exodus 20:7) and Leviticus 19:11-12.

a: The fast of the fourth month
p: Four fasts for the fall of Jerusalem, one for each of the four months named, will become feasts.
b: The four fasts keep the memory of 586 BC: the tenth month for the start of the siege (2 Kings 25:1; Jeremiah 52:4), the fourth for the breach of the city wall (Jeremiah 39:2; Jeremiah 52:6-7), the fifth for the burning of the Temple (2 Kings 25:8-9) and the seventh for the murder of Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41:1-3). The Jewish calendar keeps them as 10 Tevet, 17 Tammuz (the Mishnah dates the breach to the 17th, Taanit 4:6), 9 Av and the Fast of Gedaliah (3 Tishri). The Talmud says that when there is peace these days are feasts and when there is not they stay fasts (Rosh Hashanah 18b). Zechariah promises "joy and gladness and good feasts." The topic on the four fasts has the Christian side.
r: 2 Kings 25:1; 2 Kings 25:8-9; 2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 39:2; Jeremiah 41:1-3; Jeremiah 52:4; Zechariah 7:3; Zechariah 7:5

p: The nations come to Jerusalem to seek the LORD, as in Isaiah 2 and Micah 4.
b: The pilgrimage of the nations to Jerusalem is one of the prophets' best-known hopes: Isaiah 2:2-4 and Micah 4:1-3, then Isaiah 56:6-7 and Isaiah 60. Zechariah 14:16-19 will make it a yearly pilgrimage for the Feast of Booths. Psalm 87 names the nations as born in Zion. In the Persian period it was a hope without any sign of arrival; 8:20-23 is the book's climax, an answer to the question that began in 7:2.
r: Isaiah 2:2-4; Micah 4:1-3; Isaiah 56:6-7; Isaiah 60:3; Psalm 87; Zechariah 14:16

p: The Hebrew doubles the verb: "let us go, going." The invitation is eager.
b: Nelkhah halokh is "let us go, going," an emphatic form that means to go without delay. The city-to-city invitation, "I am going too," reads like the pilgrim's psalm, where people say "Let's go to the LORD's house" (Psalm 122:1). The same verbs, "ask the LORD's favor" and "seek the LORD of Armies," appear in 7:2, where a small delegation went to the priests. The Greek says "five cities into one" (see the variant).

a: ten men, from every tongue the nations speak
p: A picture of the nations seeking God through the Jewish people. Catholic and Reformed readings are in the note.
b: "Ten" is a full number. "Every language" (literally "all the tongues of the nations") reverses Babel, where languages were divided (Genesis 11:7-9); the nations come back together through the people of Judah. The verse says the nations will seek God through the people, not take their place: they say "we have heard that God is with you." Jews have read it as the world's future honor for Israel and its God. Paul argues in Romans 11 that Israel's story is still open. Messianic Jewish readers, described here only as a general pattern (no confession is cited), see Jews and Gentiles together. The Catholic view, in Nostra Aetate 4, is that the church draws life from the root of Israel. Calvin, on 8:23, reads the nations as drawn to worship God by the preaching of the truth, with the Jews leading because God presided over them. These do not conflict on this verse, so there is no traditions card.
r: Genesis 11:7-9; Isaiah 45:14; Isaiah 66:18-21; Romans 11:25-29; Acts 2:5-11; Zechariah 2:11; Zechariah 6:15

a: the corner of one Jew's robe
t: A Jew, and a corner of his robe
p: Yehudi is "Judean" or "Jew." The corner (kanaf) of the robe is where the tassels were.
b: Ish yehudi ("a Jewish man") appears in Jeremiah 34:9, Esther 2:5 and here: in the Persian period "Judean" and "Jew" are the same word. The Plain uses "Jew," as in Esther. The kanaf is the corner or hem; Numbers 15:38-39 commands tassels on the corners of garments to remind Israelites of the commandments, so the man whose corner they grab is visibly a Jew who keeps the law. The nations do not become Jews; they take hold of a Jew.

a: My house will be rebuilt in it
t: Claude's theory: the visions run Ezekiel 8-11 in reverse
p: Claude's reading: the visions of 1:8-6:8 answer, step by step, the departure of the glory in Ezekiel 8-11.
b: Claude's theory, resting on Ezekiel 8-11, 43 and Zechariah 1:16, 2:5, 3:1-10, 5:1-11 and 6:1-8. In Ezekiel's visions the elders worship idols in the Temple (Ezekiel 8), killers go through the city (Ezekiel 9), fire is taken from the cherubim (Ezekiel 10), and the glory of the LORD leaves by the east gate (Ezekiel 11:22-23). In Zechariah the order runs backward: heavenly riders come back into the city (1:8-17), a man measures it (2:1-5), the LORD promises to be its glory (2:5), the priest is cleansed (3), light is supplied by the LORD (4), the sins of theft and false oath are removed (5:1-4), and finally idolatry is carried off to Shinar (5:5-11). The match is rough, and the book does not claim it. The particular reversal in order is my own proposal.
r: Ezekiel 8:1-18; Ezekiel 9:1-11; Ezekiel 10:18-19; Ezekiel 11:22-23; Ezekiel 43:1-5; Zechariah 1:16; Zechariah 2:5; Zechariah 5:5-11

a: To build a house for it
t: Claude's theory: the two halves of the cleansing
p: Claude's reading: the scroll deals with people who do wrong, and the ephah deals with the system that makes wrong easy.
b: Claude's theory, resting on 5:1-4 and 5:5-11. The first vision of the pair names two persons, the thief and the one who swears falsely, and the curse goes to their houses. The second names no person: it is a measure, the standard instrument of trade, with Wickedness inside it, and it is not destroyed but exported. One way to read the pair is as two kinds of removal. Individual crimes are judged where they happen (5:4); the root that makes the crimes easy, dishonest commerce, is sent out of the land. The reading fits the prophets' habit of tying false measures to false oaths (Amos 8:5; Micah 6:10-12), and it fits the answer in 7:9-10 and 8:16-17, which is about both persons and courts. It is close to views that read the ephah as commerce and the woman as the land's corruption; I offer the "two halves" framing as my own.
r: Zechariah 5:1-4; Zechariah 5:5-11; Zechariah 7:9-10; Zechariah 8:16-17; Amos 8:5; Micah 6:10-12

t: Claude's theory: the question came from the house of God
p: Claude's reading: a pun in the delegation's name (Bethel, "house of God") may be meant: the question comes from God's own house.
b: Claude's theory, resting on 7:2-3 and Hebrew Beth-El, "house of God." The sentence can be read "Bethel sent ..." (the town) or "the house of God sent ..." The question goes to "the priests of the house of the LORD of Armies" (7:3), the Temple that was not yet finished, so a delegation is sent from a "house of God" to a "house of the LORD" to ask whether to mourn the loss of a house. The pun is not needed for the sense, and most commentators take Bethel as the town. It may be the author's play on words, as the book plays on tsemach and yitsmach (6:12). This is my own suggestion; I know of no commentator who builds on it.
